items.title: Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
items.tldr: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham travels to New York for the UN General Assembly, seeking AI cooperation and a first face‑to‑face with President Donald Trump, while unveiling a joint AI‑autonomy partnership and a historic underwater torpedo test.
items.background: Andy Burnham became UK prime minister in July 2024 and quickly signalled a proactive foreign‑policy agenda centred on technology, security and climate. His first overseas trip as head of government is to the 81st UN General Assembly in New York, where he will address the assembly on the opportunities and perils of artificial intelligence (AI). The visit also marks the inaugural face‑to‑face meeting between a UK prime minister and a US president since the 2019 Trump‑May meeting, a diplomatic milestone given the volatility of the Trump administration. In parallel, the UK and US announced a joint AI and Autonomy partnership aimed at protecting critical national infrastructure, and demonstrated a breakthrough in unmanned undersea warfare by launching a heavyweight torpedo from the Excalibur drone. The agenda is further complicated by the stalled Chagos Islands hand‑over to Mauritius, a deal that depends on US support and has been put on hold after Trump withdrew his backing.

analysis.heading: Diplomatic calculus under a volatile US presidency
analysis.content: Burnham’s public optimism about "common ground" masks a nuanced calculation. The UK‑US alliance remains the cornerstone of NATO and global security, yet Trump’s unpredictable trade and defence posture creates strategic risk. By securing a personal meeting, Burnham aims to reaffirm the "as strong as it’s ever been" narrative while extracting concessions on the Diego Garcia lease and the Chagos hand‑over. The timing—coinciding with the UN General Assembly—allows both leaders to project unity on global issues such as Ukraine and the Middle East, even as private negotiations over military basing and trade tariffs continue behind closed doors.

analysis.heading: AI governance as a diplomatic lever
analysis.content: The AI‑autonomy partnership is the centerpiece of Burnham’s UN speech. It pledges joint research on AI‑enabled protection of deep‑sea data cables, power grids and transport networks, positioning the UK as a trusted partner in the emerging "AI security" niche. At the same time, Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey’s call for a global pause on super‑intelligent AI and an International AI Safety Agency highlights internal UK debate over regulation versus innovation. By foregrounding AI cooperation, Burnham seeks to shape international norms, push for responsible LLM development, and pre‑empt a regulatory race that could marginalise European firms against US‑centric tech giants.

analysis.heading: Defense innovation and strategic signalling
analysis.content: The launch of a heavyweight torpedo from the 12‑metre Excalibur unmanned underwater vehicle marks the first such operation by either nation. This demonstration serves multiple purposes: it showcases the UK’s advanced maritime engineering, reinforces the credibility of the AI‑autonomy partnership, and sends a deterrent signal to adversaries monitoring undersea infrastructure, notably in the Strait of Hormuz and the South China Sea. The exercise also underscores a shift toward autonomous weapon systems, raising questions about command‑and‑control protocols, compliance with existing arms control regimes, and the need for transparent governance of agentic AI in lethal contexts.

key_facts: Burnham will meet President Donald Trump in New York for the first UK‑US prime‑ministerial face‑to‑face since 2019
His UN General Assembly speech will focus on AI opportunities, Ukraine peace and Middle‑East conflict resolution
The UK‑US AI and Autonomy partnership aims to protect critical national infrastructure using AI technologies
A heavyweight torpedo was launched from the British Excalibur unmanned underwater drone in a joint exercise
Negotiations over the Chagos Islands lease and Diego Garcia base remain stalled after Trump withdrew support
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey proposes a global pause on super‑intelligent AI and an International AI Safety Agency
implications: Reinforced UK‑US security cooperation could accelerate deployment of autonomous maritime weapons, prompting regional arms‑race concerns
Joint AI initiatives may shape global standards, potentially marginalising non‑Western AI firms unless inclusive governance frameworks emerge
The public meeting may smooth over friction on the Diego Garcia lease, but underlying strategic disagreements on Indo‑Pacific policy could resurface
Domestic criticism of the AI partnership could fuel UK political debate over sovereignty, tech‑industry dependence and the balance between innovation and regulation
items.outlook: In the coming months Burnham is likely to leverage the AI partnership to secure funding for UK research hubs and to lobby for an International AI Safety Agency at the UN. Parallel diplomatic tracks will aim to revive US backing for the Diego Garcia lease arrangement, while the UK will monitor Chinese and Russian responses to the unmanned torpedo test. The success of these intertwined initiatives will hinge on the durability of personal rapport between Burnham and Trump, as well as on the ability of Western policymakers to agree on a common regulatory approach to agentic AI before market fragmentation deepens.
items.fulltext:
Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
- Published
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.
The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.
The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".
"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."
Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".
Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).
He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."
The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".
He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.
His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.
Torpedo exercise
For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.
In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.
The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.
It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.
It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.
"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.
Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.
It was confirmed in April that the deal had been paused indefinitely because of Trump pulling his support.
Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.
He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.
Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.
"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."
